definition: Pittance means a very small amount, especially of money — a sum so tiny it feels unfair or insulting.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pittance. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pittance should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Pittance means a very small amount, especially of money — an intern working full weeks for a pittance may find the monthly stipend gone the moment rent is due.
A stipend is small but fair — a fixed, modest payment; a pittance is smaller still, and calling pay a pittance means it insults the work done.
A pittance at least exists; being paid nothing at all is the only step further down the scale.

Peanuts is the informal, scornful word for an insultingly small payment — 'they work for peanuts.' It belongs to casual speech and always sounds dismissive. Pittance means the same unfairly small sum but fits formal writing: reporters and historians write that laborers earned a pittance, not peanuts.

A trifle is a thing or matter of no importance — a knickknack, a small worry you wave away. Pittance is angrier and specifically about money: pay so small it shortchanges real work. You shrug off a trifle; you resent a pittance.

A song, in the fixed phrase 'for a song,' means a laughably small price — a house bought or sold for a song. It is about bargain prices, not wages. A pittance is what someone is paid for work, and the word accuses the payer of unfairness.

From the same Latin root pietas comes piety — devotion to duty or religion; a pittance began as a small gift of food donated to monks out of piety.
Pittance means a very small amount, especially of money — a sum so tiny it feels unfair or insulting.
The magazine offered Lena a pittance for her two-thousand-word article — fifteen dollars, less than she had spent on lunch while researching it.
Fifteen dollars for weeks of research and writing is an insultingly small payment.
Comparing the fee to the cost of a single lunch makes the tininess of the sum concrete — that is a pittance.

Pittance almost always carries indignation about money: workers are 'paid a pittance,' heirlooms are 'sold for a pittance.' It implies the amount is unfairly small, not just small — you wouldn't call a reasonable discount a pittance.

Every October, the orchard outside Dunmore hires forty pickers for the harvest.
The work is brutal: ladders before dawn, bushel after bushel, shoulders burning by noon.
For years the pay was a pittance — a few cents a bushel, so little that a full week of climbing barely covered a picker's bus fare and boots.
Then a picker taped her pay slip to the co-op notice board, next to the price of a single apple downtown, and people did the math themselves.
The next season, the orchard doubled the rate.
The fruit cost pennies more; the ladders felt the same, but the paychecks finally answered the work.
